0.0.n: Used to open the broadcast and get listeners’ attention, rather than to answer a question.

0.2.n: さん makes this a polite way to address the audience.

0.3.n: This evening greeting ends with は, pronounced わ.

1.1.n: Describes the Japanese as easy to understand, not gentle or kind here.

1.2.n: Refers to the language and forms part of the program’s title.

1.3.n: An English borrowing written in katakana, used here in the program’s title.

1.4.n: Part of the program’s name; わん also represents a dog’s bark in Japanese.

1.6.n: Links the program’s title to 時間, identifying which program it is time for.

1.7.n: The pattern の時間です announces that it is time for something.

1.8.n: Adds a polite ending to the announcement.

2.0.n: Must come directly before a noun; here it points to the current news program.

2.1.n: Refers to the broadcast being introduced, rather than one individual news story.

2.2.n: Marks this news program as the topic; the explanation continues over the following lines.

2.4.n: The name of Japan’s public broadcaster, used within the news service’s title.

2.6.n: An English word forming part of the service name NHK NEWS WEB EASY.

2.8.n: Part of the service’s English name, referring to its online format.

2.10.n: Part of the service’s English name, indicating accessible Japanese.

2.11.n: Shows that NHK NEWS WEB EASY is one example, not the only source.

2.12.n: Links these sources to the news described in the next line.

3.0.n: Modifies 日本語 to describe language that learners can understand more readily.

3.1.n: Names the language used to write the news.

3.2.n: Marks the language used for writing.

3.3.n: Past passive form of 書く: the news received the action of writing.

3.4.n: The preceding phrase describes this noun: news written in easy Japanese.

3.5.n: Connects examples in a list without implying that the list is complete.

4.0.n: Describes stories that catch the speaker’s interest; it does not necessarily mean funny.

4.1.n: Refers to additional stories the speaker finds interesting.

4.2.n: Marks the listed news as what the speaker looks at.

4.3.n: て-form of 見る, linking looking at the news to the thoughts and speaking that follow.

5.0.n: The speaker identifies themself immediately afterward as ニュース犬.

5.2.n: The speaker’s name or persona; 犬 means dog.

5.3.n: Marks 私、ニュース犬 as the person who had the thoughts.

5.4.n: Past form of 思う, modifying こと to describe what the speaker thought.

5.5.n: Turns 思った into a noun phrase: the things the speaker thought.

5.6.n: Marks the speaker’s thoughts as the content they will share.

5.7.n: Politely addresses all the viewers or listeners.

5.8.n: Marks the audience as the recipients of the speaker’s words.

5.9.n: Polite form of 話す, describing what the speaker will do in this program.

0.tip: 皆さん is a friendly, polite way to address a whole audience.

1.lit: It is time for Easy Japanese News Wan.
1.tip: The pattern Xの時間です means it is time for X.

2.lit: As for this news program, from NHK NEWS WEB EASY and similar sources…
2.tip: The final の connects the sources here to ニュース in the next line.

3.lit: News written in easy Japanese, and…
3.tip: Japanese puts descriptions before nouns: やさしい日本語で書かれた describes ニュース.

4.tip: 見て links this action to what follows instead of ending the sentence.

5.lit: What I, News Dog, thought, to everyone I will tell.
5.tip: 思ったこと means what the speaker thought; こと lets a verb phrase function like a noun.
